entries.clue: Gather heat is on the rise (5,2)

blocks.note: a heat is a round of a competition
something on the rise is up

annotation.surface: A worried report that things are getting hotter, perhaps in a kitchen or a crisis.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Heat' looks like temperature, but here it is a qualifying round in a race or contest.
annotation.definitionFit: A phrasal-verb synonym: rounding up cattle or suspects means collecting them in one place.

entries.clue: Discover doctor breaking law (6)

indicatorNotes.breaking: to break something is to split it open, so the law is broken apart for the doctor to sit inside

blocks.note: a law is a rule
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's degree

annotation.surface: A physician caught flouting the law.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Breaking' reads as breaking the law, but it is the doctor physically breaking into the word. MB is a medical degree, so it stands for a doctor.
annotation.definitionFit: A British slang sense: to rumble a plot or a person is to see through it and find out the truth.

entries.clue: Neglected old Germans suspended heartlessly (6)

indicatorNotes.heartlessly: meant here as cruelly, without mercy, and applied as losing the head letter H from each word, as 'headlessly' would say more exactly

blocks.note: HUNS, an old word for Germans, without its H
HUNG, without its H

annotation.surface: A grim scene of forgotten Germans hanged without mercy.
annotation.walkthrough: Both words lose their first letter, H, although 'heartlessly' would normally mean losing the middle; read it as the setter's loose way of saying 'without heads'.
annotation.definitionFit: Unsung heroes are neglected ones, whose deeds were never praised in song.

entries.clue: Squalid mix of skin and ice (10)

indicatorNotes.mix of: a mix is a blend, so the letters are stirred together into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

annotation.surface: A grubby, freezing scene: a nasty blend of skin and ice.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole phrase 'skin and ice' is the fodder, including the 'and'.
annotation.definitionFit: Named after a writer: Dickensian describes the squalid slums and workhouses of Charles Dickens's novels.

entries.clue: Said to invest heavily in support for electricity grid (5)

indicatorNotes.Said: what is said is spoken, so we want the sound of the phrase, not its spelling

blocks.note: to pile money on a bet or venture is to invest heavily in it

annotation.surface: A report of big investment in the national power network.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as financial news, and the investment talk is itself the sound clue: PILE ON, spoken, is PYLON.
annotation.definitionFit: A description by function: a pylon is the steel lattice tower that holds up overhead power cables.

entries.clue: Concierge takes time removing new floor cover (7)

indicatorNotes.takes: to take something is to pick it up and carry it along, so the concierge acquires the time letter
indicatorNotes.removing: to remove is to take away, so the letter for new comes out of the concierge

blocks.note: a doorman, the hotel porter at the entrance
N = new, removed from the end of DOORMAN
T = time

annotation.surface: A hotel concierge taking his time to take away a new rug.
annotation.walkthrough: N for new is the standard abbreviation; it comes off the end of DOORMAN before T goes on.
annotation.definitionFit: A description by function: a doormat is the mat laid on the floor at a door to wipe feet on.

entries.clue: Damage trip had on intimate (4,1,4)

indicatorNotes.Damage: something damaged is broken out of shape, so the letters are knocked into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

annotation.surface: Someone asking what harm a trip did to a close friend.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Intimate' looks like an adjective meaning close, but it is the verb, stressed on the last syllable.
annotation.definitionFit: A synonym for the verb: to intimate is to suggest something indirectly rather than state it.

entries.clue: Get rid of French author that’s rejected publicity (4)

indicatorNotes.that’s rejected: something rejected is thrown out, so the publicity letters are thrown out of the author

blocks.note: Marcel Proust, the French novelist
PR = public relations, removed from the front of PROUST

annotation.surface: A French writer turning down publicity and being dropped.
annotation.walkthrough: PR, public relations, stands for publicity; take it off the front of PROUST.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to oust someone is to force them out of a place or post.

entries.clue: Dish causing tension during dinner with fool (4,4)

indicatorNotes.during: during means in the middle of, so the tension letter goes inside the dinner
indicatorNotes.with: with means alongside, so the fool is added on after

blocks.note: T = tension, as in physics
dinner is a meal; T goes in after ME
an oaf is a fool

annotation.surface: An awkward dinner party made tense by a foolish guest.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dish' is not the cause of tension in the story but the definition; 'causing' just joins it to the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: meat loaf is a dish of minced meat baked in a loaf shape.

entries.clue: Little Edward accepts present is tied up (8)

indicatorNotes.accepts: to accept something is to take it in, so TED takes the other word inside itself

blocks.note: Ted is short for Edward
present = there, as in answering a roll call

annotation.surface: A little boy accepting a gift that has been tied up with ribbon.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Present' looks like a gift, but it means being there.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a tethered animal is tied up on a rope to a post.

entries.clue: Notes from Greek character – as written (5)

blocks.note: mu, the Greek letter M
sic, Latin for 'thus', marks a quotation as written

annotation.surface: Written notes from a Greek person, quoted exactly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Notes' looks like messages, but it is musical notes.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by component: music is what a string of notes makes.

entries.clue: Where glances may be traded quickly! (4,5)

blocks.note: glances are looks, and a mart is a market, so a place for trading them
an order to hurry up, as a sergeant might bark

annotation.surface: A playful question of where you could buy and sell glances.
annotation.walkthrough: Split the answer differently, LOOKS MART, to see the market in glances; 'look smart!' is a British command to hurry.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: 'look smart!' is a British command to get a move on, so it means quickly.

entries.clue: It illuminates talk depicting prominent facial feature (7,3)

blocks.note: a lantern gives light
to jaw is to talk at length

annotation.surface: A spotlit conversation that shows off someone's striking face.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Jaw' as slang for talk is informal, as in 'stop jawing'.
annotation.definitionFit: A description: a lantern jaw is a long, jutting jaw that dominates a face.

entries.clue: Naughty introductions for burlesque leave us excited (4)

indicatorNotes.introductions for: an introduction comes at the start, so each word gives only its opening letter

blocks.note: first letters of Burlesque Leave Us Excited

annotation.surface: A burlesque show leaving the audience excited by its naughtiness.
annotation.walkthrough: Blue means risqué or smutty, as in a blue joke; the surface is itself naughty.
annotation.definitionFit: A colour sense: blue jokes and blue films are sexually naughty.

entries.clue: Spits on formal hat – sweet! (10)

blocks.note: to gob is British slang for to spit
a topper is a top hat

annotation.surface: Someone spitting on a top hat, and delighted about it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sweet!' looks like an exclamation of approval; it is the British word for a candy. A gobstopper is a very large hard round sweet.
annotation.definitionFit: A British sweet: a gobstopper is a hard ball of candy big enough to stop your gob (mouth).

entries.clue: To get away from people, doctor flies to Sale (4,7)

indicatorNotes.doctor: to doctor is to tamper with or falsify, so the letters are altered into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

annotation.surface: A doctor escaping people by flying off to Sale.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like a person, but it is the verb, to tamper with. Sale is a town near Manchester.
annotation.definitionFit: A paraphrase: to self-isolate is to keep yourself away from other people, as in a pandemic.

entries.clue: Policy to have Tiber redirected – that’s depraved (9)

indicatorNotes.to have: to have something is to hold it, so the policy word holds the other letters
indicatorNotes.redirected: redirected means sent a different way, so the river's letters change direction and order

blocks.note: a line is a policy, as in the party line
the Tiber, the river through Rome, rearranged

annotation.surface: A decadent plan to reroute Rome's river.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Policy' looks like the definition at the head of the clue, but the definition is 'depraved' at the end; the Tiber is the river through Rome.
annotation.definitionFit: An adjective sense: libertine, usually a noun for a rake, also describes dissolute, depraved behaviour.

entries.clue: One is an exhibitionist out of habit (8)

annotation.definition: One is an exhibitionist out of habit

blocks.note: someone who shows off their body in public
a habit is also a garment, as a nun wears, so this means out of their clothes, not from routine

annotation.surface: A person who shows off by force of habit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Out of habit' seems to mean from routine, but a habit is a garment; the exhibitionist is naked, and a STREAKER runs naked in public.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by description: a streaker is an exhibitionist who dashes naked across a sports ground or public place.

entries.clue: Setter and solver make alternative version of us (2,3,3)

blocks.note: the setter speaks of himself as 'me' and addresses the solver as 'you'
two people together are 'us', said the long way

annotation.surface: A friendly remark from the setter about the two people doing this puzzle.
annotation.walkthrough: In crosswords the setter often calls himself 'me' and the solver 'you'; put together, they spell out the long form of 'us'.
annotation.definitionFit: A paraphrase: the setter and the solver are the two people meant by 'us', each named in turn.

entries.clue: Murderous Scottish couple attach odd batches to them (3,8)

indicatorNotes.attach: to attach is to fasten one thing onto another, so the two parts are joined end to end
indicatorNotes.odd: odd means strange or out of true, so the batches' letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: used as it is
BATCHES rearranged

annotation.surface: A murderous Scottish pair adding strange batches of something to their victims.
annotation.walkthrough: The anagrammed batches go after 'them', not the other way round.
annotation.definitionFit: A literary reference: Macbeth and Lady Macbeth are the murderous couple in Shakespeare's Scottish play.

entries.clue: Sign church is involved in waste (6)

indicatorNotes.is involved in: to be involved in something is to be caught up inside it, so the church letters sit inside the waste

blocks.note: CE = Church of England
piss is a crude word for urine, bodily waste

annotation.surface: A sign that the church is mixed up in wastefulness.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sign' looks like an omen, but it is a sign of the zodiac.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: Pisces, the Fish, is one of the twelve signs of the zodiac.

entries.clue: Imagine writer producing uplifting piece of meditation on Nelson (6)

indicatorNotes.uplifting: in a down clue, lifting up means reading from bottom to top, so backwards
indicatorNotes.piece of: a piece is only part, so the letters are a run taken from within the words

blocks.note: the run NON NEL from meditatioN ON NELson

annotation.surface: Someone imagining an author writing an inspiring meditation on Admiral Nelson.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Imagine' looks like a verb, but it is John Lennon's song title.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by work: John Lennon wrote the song Imagine.

entries.clue: Recognise oddly missing periods of time (4)

indicatorNotes.oddly missing: the odd-numbered letters go missing, leaving the even ones

blocks.note: the even letters of rEcOgNiSe

annotation.surface: Failing to recognise someone after a long time apart.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' seems to describe the failure to recognise, but it picks out letters 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 to drop.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: eons are immeasurably long ages.

entries.clue: One walking round bar to find bouncer (10)

blocks.note: a tramp walks, and to tramp is to walk
O is round
a bar is a line

annotation.surface: Someone walking round a pub looking for the doorman.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bouncer' looks like a pub doorman, and 'bar' like a pub; it is a thing you bounce on.
annotation.definitionFit: A playful sense: a trampoline is what bounces you into the air, so it is a bouncer.

entries.clue: Artist has working method that’s clear (5)

blocks.note: MO = modus operandi, a way of working
net pay is what is clear of deductions

annotation.surface: A painter with a lucid way of working.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Clear' looks like lucid, but it means net, as in clearing a profit; MO is the modus operandi of police dramas.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Claude Monet was the French Impressionist painter of the water lilies.

entries.clue: In the middle of desert, family creates a suburban home (4)

indicatorNotes.In the middle of: the middle of a word is its central letters, and here it applies to both words

blocks.note: the middle of deSErt
the middle of faMIly

annotation.surface: A family out in the desert making a home like one in the suburbs.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In the middle of' seems to place the family in the desert, but it applies to both words. A semi is a semi-detached house, typical of British suburbs.
annotation.definitionFit: A British abbreviation: a semi is a semi-detached house, one of a joined pair, the classic suburban home.

entries.clue: Yankees in turmoil due to such economic policies? (9)

annotation.definitionNote: KEYNESIAN is an adjective describing such policies

indicatorNotes.turmoil: turmoil is confusion and disorder, so the letters are thrown about

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

annotation.surface: Americans left in chaos by some economic programme.
annotation.walkthrough: The 'in' belongs to the fodder, not the indicator.
annotation.definitionFit: Named after an economist: Keynesian policies follow John Maynard Keynes in using government spending to manage demand.

entries.clue: Able to follow exercise nut? (5)

indicatorNotes.to follow: to follow is to come after, so the word for able is placed after the exercise letters

blocks.note: PE = physical education
able = can

annotation.surface: Wondering whether someone can keep up with a fitness fanatic.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Nut' looks like a fanatic, as in fitness nut; it is the plain nut.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the pecan is a North American nut, as in pecan pie.

entries.clue: Dull path around home (7)

indicatorNotes.around: around means encircling, so the path wraps round the word for home

blocks.note: a route is a path
at home = in

annotation.surface: A boring walk around the house.
annotation.walkthrough: IN, as in 'staying in', is a standard stand-in for home.
annotation.definitionFit: An adjective sense: routine work is dull because it never varies.

entries.clue: Surrenders and retires (5,2)

blocks.note: hands over to the authorities, as a weapon or a fugitive
goes to bed for the night

annotation.surface: Someone who gives up and goes to bed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Retires' looks like leaving work, but it means going to bed.
annotation.definitionFit: Two phrasal-verb senses: to turn in a weapon is to hand it over, and to turn in is also to go to bed.
